title: Tests for unsaturation, and alcoholic, phenolic, aldehydic, ketonic, carboxylic and amino groups
objective: Apply bromine-water and Baeyer's tests to detect carbon-carbon unsaturation
Distinguish alcohols, phenols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids using selective reagents
Recognise that 2,4-DNP is positive for BOTH aldehydes and ketones, requiring a further test to distinguish them
Detect a primary aromatic amine by diazotisation and dye coupling

theory.statement: Each functional group reacts selectively with a particular reagent, giving a distinctive colour change, precipitate, or gas that identifies it. Applying the RIGHT reagent to the RIGHT compound, and interpreting a negative result as meaningfully as a positive one, is the skill being examined.
theory.derivationNote: Some tests are class tests (positive for a whole family, e.g. 2,4-DNP for any carbonyl), while others discriminate within a family (Tollens'/Fehling's positive for aldehydes but not ketones, since only an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon still bears a removable hydrogen that can be oxidised). Similarly, neutral FeCl3 detects a phenol's acidic -OH by complex formation, but a carboxylic acid — also acidic — gives no such colour and is instead detected by effervescence with NaHCO3, since only a carboxylic acid is a strong enough acid to liberate CO2 from bicarbonate.
keyEquations: Alkene + Br2 → vicinal dibromide (decolourises bromine water)
RCHO + 2Cu2+(complexed) + 5OH- → RCOO- + Cu2O↓(brick red) + 3H2O (Fehling's, aldehyde only)
RCOOH + NaHCO3 → RCOONa + H2O + CO2↑ (carboxylic acid)

apparatus.name: Bromine water
apparatus.why: Tests for carbon-carbon unsaturation by addition

apparatus.name: Tollens' reagent, Fehling's solution
apparatus.why: Selective for aldehydes (oxidise them), negative for ketones

apparatus.name: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine reagent
apparatus.why: General test for any carbonyl (aldehyde or ketone)

apparatus.name: Sodium bicarbonate solution
apparatus.why: Detects a carboxylic acid by effervescence of CO2

apparatus.name: Sodium nitrite, dilute HCl, β-naphthol
apparatus.why: Diazotisation/coupling test for a primary aromatic amine

procedure.text: Select a compound and a reagent thought to match its suspected functional group.
Add the reagent and note the observation (colour, precipitate, gas, odour).
Repeat for at least four different compound/reagent combinations, including at least one expected negative.
Tabulate which functional group each positive result confirms.

steps: Match each reagent to the group it tests for
Record the observation for each compound tested
Tally which functional groups were correctly identified

expectedResult.quantity: Functional groups correctly identified from the compounds tested
expectedResult.statement: Each reagent gives a positive result only with the compound bearing its target functional group: bromine water/Baeyer's for unsaturation, ceric ammonium nitrate for the alcohol, FeCl3 for the phenol, Tollens'/Fehling's for the aldehyde (not the ketone), 2,4-DNP for both carbonyls, NaHCO3 for the acid, and diazotisation-coupling for the primary aromatic amine.

safety: Bromine water and concentrated acids are corrosive/irritating — handle with care and good ventilation.
Tollens' reagent must not be stored — it can form an explosive silver residue on standing; prepare fresh and discard promptly after use.
Aniline is toxic — avoid skin contact.
sourcesOfError: Using a stale or wrongly prepared Fehling's/Tollens' reagent gives a false negative.
Confusing the general carbonyl test (2,4-DNP) with the aldehyde-specific tests (Tollens'/Fehling's) leads to misassigning ketones as aldehydes.
A phenol's mild acidity is sometimes mistaken for carboxylic-acid acidity — the NaHCO3 test distinguishes them, since phenol is too weak an acid to liberate CO2 from bicarbonate.

viva.question: Why does Fehling's solution distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone, when both are carbonyl compounds?
viva.expectedConcept: An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon bears a hydrogen atom that can be removed on oxidation to give a carboxylic acid, reducing Cu2+ to Cu2O in the process. A ketone's carbonyl carbon has no such hydrogen and cannot be oxidised this way, so it gives no reaction.
viva.answerLogic: Only an aldehyde's C-H at the carbonyl carbon permits this oxidation.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking any carbonyl compound reduces Fehling's solution.

viva.question: A compound is acidic to litmus but gives no colour with neutral FeCl3. What does this suggest?
viva.expectedConcept: It is likely a carboxylic acid rather than a phenol — both are acidic, but only phenols give the characteristic FeCl3 colour (forming an iron-phenolate complex); carboxylic acids do not. The NaHCO3 effervescence test would confirm a carboxylic acid.
viva.answerLogic: FeCl3 is phenol-selective among acidic organics.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming FeCl3 detects acidity in general rather than the phenolic -OH specifically.

viva.question: Why is 2,4-DNP alone not sufficient to identify a compound as an aldehyde?
viva.expectedConcept: 2,4-DNP forms a coloured precipitate with ANY carbonyl compound — aldehyde or ketone alike — so a positive result only proves a C=O group is present, not which kind; a further test (Tollens'/Fehling's) is needed to tell them apart.
viva.answerLogic: 2,4-DNP is a class test, not a discriminating one.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating a positive 2,4-DNP result as proof of an aldehyde specifically.

preLab.question: Which reagent gives a positive test for BOTH aldehydes and ketones?
preLab.feedback: 2,4-DNP is a general carbonyl test; Tollens' and Fehling's are aldehyde-selective.

duringLab.question: Test at least four compound/reagent combinations.

postLab.question: A carboxylic acid can be distinguished from a phenol by:
postLab.feedback: Only a carboxylic acid is a strong enough acid to release CO2 from sodium bicarbonate; phenol is not.
